newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian leaders relieved by Chechnya vote outcome.
newsitem.headline: Russian leaders relieved by Chechnya vote outcome.

text.p: Aslan Maskhadov's probable victory in Chechnya's presidential election on Tuesday is a huge relief for Russian leaders, giving them a trusted partner at potentially explosive talks on the rebel region's future.

But even under the leadership of the relatively moderate former guerrilla commander, Chechnya remains a big problem for Russian President Boris Yeltsin. He and Maskhadov will have to tread carefully to prevent the conflict flaring again.
Electoral officials said partial counts showed Maskhadov would clear the 50 percent of votes needed to avoid a second ballot. Radical guerrilla leader Shamil Basayev was second.

"Chechnya now has a legitimate power and Russia has a partner to talk to -- its preferred partner, although that does not mean that talks will be easy," said Andrei Piontkowski, head of the Centre for Strategic Studies think tank in Moscow.
"I do not see any new hostilities breaking out now. But if hawkish Russian politicians take control in Moscow, the situation could be different in five years."

The agreement last August which ended 21 months of fighting between Russian troops and Chechen separatists gave the two sides a five-year breathing space before solving the dispute at the heart of the conflict -- whether Chechnya is in Russia.
The Chechens say they have won de facto independence and want Russia to recognise it officially. Moscow has offered Chechnya a high degree of autonomy but has ruled out secession.
The talks will clearly not be easy. The risk of them collapsing and fighting resuming at some time cannot be ignored, even though clashes seem unlikely in the near future.
Maskhadov, and the other 12 presidential candidates, vowed to take on the Kremlin over the sovereignty issue. He also promised to press hard for war reparations.

Russian officials spoke highly of Maskhadov during peace negotiations last year and they regard him as more trustworthy than his rivals, particularly Basayev who is wanted in Russia for commanding a bloody hostage-taking raid in 1995.

"Moscow will count on Maskhadov not going too far with his demands and that he will not try to humiliate Russia too much," said Viktor Kremenyuk, deputy head of the independent USA and Canada Institute, another Moscow think tank.
"He will be under pressure from radicals in Chechnya to take a firm line over independence, but the fact that he has been elected for five years gives him legitimacy and freedom to act."
Both sides have an interest in avoiding a resumption of the fighting and any extreme rhetoric which could jeopardise their fragile relations.
The Kremlin wants to be tough enough to avoid encouraging other independent-minded regions to try to secede but it also wants stability on its southern flank.
Yeltsin, his nose bloodied by the guerrilla army which eventually forced his troops to withdraw, appears to believe war is almost unwinnable and politically inadvisable.
The Chechens value maintaining good relations because they will depend on Russia for money and business to rebuild their economy, shattered by the war.

Maskhadov's initial task will be to rally Chechens around him without spoiling his relatively good ties with Russian leaders. But economic issues, and Chechnya's role as an oil-refining centre, will never be far from his mind.

"You cannot expect Maskhadov to express really tough views now for independence or, on the other hand, on strengthening ties with Moscow," said political analyst Sergei Markov of the Moscow office of the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace.

"His main task is to restore order and consolidate the Chechen people around him. He has to approach the people who control the arms and the oil -- no economic projects will be possible if small bands of men control the oil."
The Kremlin is already using economic leverage to try to ensure peace and keep Chechnya in Russia. Some analysts believe oil is vital to the strategy.
Chechnya has a pipeline running through it and is a possible transit point for future pipelines carrying oil through that part of southern Russia.
Russia has already promised funds for rebuilding plans which include Chechnya's oil refineries. Those resources, and the pipelines issue, could be vital for keeping relations on track.
